report:
Based on the retrieved evidence, **your hypothesis appears to be incorrect** — the evidence strongly suggests that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) *does* increase HIV testing uptake, though it may not proportionally increase new HIV diagnoses.

**Evidence for increased testing uptake:**

Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials converge on this conclusion. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs among key populations found that "distribution of free HIVST kits increases the uptake of HIV testing when compared to standard of care among key populations overall and in all sub-group analyses" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z). Similarly, a 2021 Lancet eClinicalMedicine systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of HIVST compared to standard testing services and built on earlier evidence that informed the WHO's 2016 recommendation supporting self-testing (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext). A separate 2021 PLOS ONE systematic review and meta-analysis focused on adults in Africa similarly examined effects of HIVST on testing uptake, linkage to treatment, and social harms (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498).

**An important nuance:**

While uptake increases, this doesn't always translate to more diagnoses. One source notes: "a randomized controlled trial from the UK and a meta-analysis...similarly found that HIVSTs led to a larger volume of testing but no additional HIV diagnoses" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23259582251393357).

**Conclusion:** The weight of RCT evidence and multiple meta-analyses indicates that offering HIV self-testing does increase the number of people who test for HIV, particularly among underserved groups like men and key populations — though it may not proportionally increase the number of positive diagnoses found.
